KEY MESSAGE 1...Cool and unsettled with periods of lake enhanced 
rain showers through Monday morning.

A mid level closed low will move from the Gulf of Maine this morning 
to the Canadian Maritimes this afternoon, with moist cyclonic flow 
rapidly moving away as a narrow mid level ridge axis briefly crosses 
the eastern Great Lakes. A few showers across Central NY and the
North Country early this morning will end by mid morning. Clouds
will give way to rapid clearing from west to east this morning
before the next round of clouds increase this afternoon.

Another fast moving and potent mid level trough will dig from the 
upper Great Lakes this evening to New England by Monday, with an 
associated cold front crossing the eastern Great Lakes tonight. The 
airmass is still cool enough to support a lake response even ahead 
of the cold front. Expect a few lake effect rain showers to develop 
east/northeast of the lakes late this afternoon and this evening as 
large scale forcing and synoptic scale moisture increase, and 
improve the background lake effect environment. Initial development 
will be near Buffalo and Watertown on WSW flow.

Boundary layer flow will veer to the WNW tonight and NW by Monday 
morning, carrying lake effect and lake enhanced rain showers 
southeast of the lakes. Synoptic scale forcing will be strong enough 
to support scattered to numerous showers even outside of lake effect 
areas overnight through early Monday. Lake enhancement will bring 
steadier rain and higher QPF east and southeast of the lakes, with 
the highest rain amounts across the Tug Hill Plateau and Oswego 
County. A few locations may pick up 0.50" to 0.75" of rain, with the 
steady translation of lake effect bands southward in veering wind 
profiles preventing any higher totals. Boundary layer and surface 
temps stay plenty warm enough for all liquid, although a few 
locations may see some graupel or small hail in convective lake 
effect showers.

Showers will continue through Monday morning, especially southeast 
of the lakes from ongoing lake enhancement and upslope flow. The mid 
level trough and associated deeper moisture will then pull away in 
the afternoon, with showers gradually ending from west to east. The 
last of the showers across Central NY and the higher terrain of the 
North Country will mostly end by mid to late afternoon.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Gusty winds today, especially across Western NY.

A tight pressure gradient will remain in place today across the 
Great Lakes as a potent mid level trough and associated cold front 
approach from the northwest. Forecast model soundings show a belt of 
35 to 45 knots in the 2K to 5K layer, with lapse rates steepening 
sufficiently this afternoon to support mixing of stronger winds down 
to the surface. BUFKIT momentum transfer schemes and other model 
guidance suggests that gusts will stay just below advisory criteria, 
with peak gusts in the 40 to 45 mph range northeast of Lake Erie 
from the Niagara Frontier to near Rochester this afternoon. 
Elsewhere, gusts will be in the 20 to 30 mph range today.

It will stay windy tonight through Monday morning, with boundary 
layer flow gradually veering to the WNW overnight. Gusts of 25 to 35 
mph will be common across the entire region, with some 40 mph gusts 
possible across the higher terrain of the Southern Tier and Finger 
Lakes.

KEY MESSAGE 3...Colder and unsettled weather returns late in the 
week, with some wet snow potential.

Mainly dry and somewhat warmer weather will return Tuesday through 
Wednesday, with just a chance of a few light showers each day across 
the North Country as a series of shortwaves cross southern Canada. 

The pattern becomes much more interesting Thursday through Saturday 
as a deep trough carves out over the Great Lakes, evolving into a 
broad closed low across the eastern Great Lakes and New England by 
Friday. Shortwave phasing from the upstream split flow regime will 
likely support surface low development across the Ohio Valley by 
Thursday, with a maturing system moving towards the Mid Atlantic and 
New England by Friday and Saturday.

Rain chances will increase Thursday through Thursday night as the 
system approaches. Colder air will be drawn southward through the 
Great Lakes as the trough deepens, which will eventually introduce 
the potential for a change from rain to wet snow by Friday and 
Saturday. The airmass is not particularly cold, so if a change to 
wet snow does occur amounts will likely be highly elevation 
dependent.

Forecast confidence is high on a turn towards chilly, unsettled 
weather at the end of the week, but there is very low confidence 
with wet snow potential, and this will continue to be the case for 
at least several more days. An ensemble approach is prudent, and
